docs.text: Sequence preparation (development notes) ¶ Base52 short-name hashing ¶ Prepare Sequences builds short names (<=32 characters by default) in the frontend ( frontend/src/stores/shortName.ts ). Several strategies embed a fixed-length base52 token from hashBase52 . The pattern strategy uses one set-wide uid derived from sorted prepared DNA strings; stem, regex, and split strategies hash each row's original_aa (pre-tag amino acid sequence), falling back to design_id if empty. 1. Hash primitive (UTF-8, FNV-1a 64, base52) ¶ Encode the input string as UTF-8 bytes. Compute a 64-bit FNV-1a hash (offset basis 14695981039346656037 , prime 1099511628211 ), XORing and multiplying per byte, masked to 64 bits. Convert the 64-bit integer to L characters with base52(value, L) using the 52-symbol alphabet ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz . Each step takes value mod 52 and integer-divides by 52, then reverses the digits so the output reads most-significant digit first at fixed width L . The exported helper is: hashBase52(input: string, length: number) := base52(fnv1a64(input), length) In code, base52 clamps L to 1..32 . Strategies that expose "hash length" or "UID length" in the UI use clampHashLen , which restricts lengths to 3..10 for Prepare Sequences short names. Changing UID or hash length adjusts how many base52 characters are emitted without changing the hash algorithm. Longer lengths include more of the 64-bit digest (fewer collisions, longer strings); shorter lengths truncate to the leading (most-significant) base52 digits of the same 64-bit value. 2. Pattern strategy (UID length) ¶ In the pattern strategy, all rows in the current prepared set share the same middle token ( uid ), computed from the multiset of nucleotide strings in the set: Take each row's prepared_dna , or '' if DNA is not available yet. Sort those strings lexicographically ( localeCompare ). Join with record separator \x1e . Compute uid = hashBase52(joined, uidLength) with uidLength clamped to 3..10 . The uid changes when any row's prepared DNA changes, when rows are added or removed, or when duplicate counts of identical DNA strings change. Amino acid sequences and design_id are not included in the input. The final short name is prefix_uid_index (optional prefix, shared uid , and 1-based row index with optional zero padding), truncated to the global max length. 3. Per-row amino acid hash strategies ¶ These strategies compute hashBase52(original_aa || design_id, hashLen) with hashLen clamped to 3..10 : Smart: stem + hash (when "Include hash" is enabled) Smart: Regex drop prefix / suffix (suffix hash after stem) Split + take indices (when "Add hash" is enabled) Matching original_aa (or design_id ) values with the same hashLen generate the same hash segment; uniqueify in shortName.ts deduplicates final short names afterward. A duplicate design_id in the current set triggers a "Long name not unique" warning. A duplicate pre-suffix short name triggers a "Short name not unique" warning on all rows in the colliding group, including the unsuffixed row. Both warnings appear in the warnings column and the "less than ideal" banner, and highlight the Short name panel border in red. Rows given an _N suffix also display the auto-dedupe warning inside that panel. 4. Strategy summary ¶ Concept UI / field Clamped length hashBase52 input Pattern uid UID length 3-10 Sorted list of prepared_dna (empty if missing), joined with \x1e Stem / regex / split hash Hash length (base52) 3-10 original_aa or design_id if AA missing computeSetFingerprint remains in shortName.ts as an exported helper for other stable-set digests if needed; pattern uids do not use it. Implementation reference: frontend/src/stores/shortName.ts ( fnv1a64 , base52 , hashBase52 , computeShortNames , rawNameForRow ).

docs.text: Development setup ¶ Binderdash is a single-page app with two parts: Frontend: Vite + Vue 3 (Composition API) + PrimeVue, with the Mol* structure viewer and Vega-Lite plots. Backend: FastAPI (async), serving the REST API and the built frontend as static files. AGENTS.md in the repository root defines the code-style, environment-variable, and release rules. Prerequisites ¶ Python 3.11+ (tested with 3.12) uv (Python package manager and runner) Node.js 18+ and pnpm Docker (optional, for the containerised workflow) Repository layout ¶ Path Contents backend/ FastAPI app; the frontend build is written to backend/static/ backend/config/ Per-pipeline detection and display rules (see Adding a pipeline method type ) frontend/ Vite + Vue SPA source desktop/ pywebview + PyInstaller desktop packaging (see desktop/README.md ) docs/ This documentation (MkDocs) tests/ Playwright end-to-end tests (backend unit tests are in backend/tests/ ) example_runs/ Example run data (optional, not in git) Environment configuration ¶ Binderdash loads configuration from .env at the repository root. Copy .env.example as a starting point; it documents all supported variables. For local development, the defaults (authentication disabled, SQLite under data/ , runs from ./example_runs ) are usually sufficient. To create a local user account instead, set DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" and add a bcrypt hash to LOCAL_USERS : python backend/scripts/encrypt_password.py myusername # prompts for the password See Authentication for the other sign-in providers. Backend ¶ Create a virtual environment and install dependencies: uv venv -p python3.12 .venv && source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -r backend/requirements.txt If a conda environment is active, deactivate it first so it does not shadow the venv. Start the API server with auto-reload: uv run uvicorn backend.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 The server listens on http://localhost:8000 . Changing backend dependencies ¶ After modifying backend/pyproject.toml , regenerate and install the pinned requirements: uv pip compile backend/pyproject.toml -o backend/requirements.txt uv pip install -r backend/requirements.txt Frontend ¶ You can run the frontend in two modes. To rebuild into backend/static/ automatically (recommended while the backend is running so FastAPI on :8000 serves the latest build): cd frontend pnpm install pnpm run watch:build To run the Vite dev server with hot reload on http://localhost:5173 (proxying API calls to the backend): cd frontend pnpm install pnpm run dev For a one-off production build, run pnpm run build in frontend/ . Docker development mode ¶ docker-compose.dev.yml runs the backend with auto-reload and a separate container that rebuilds the frontend when Vue/TypeScript files change. The project directory is mounted from your filesystem. Because the frontend container rebuilds backend/static/ and the backend container updates data/ inside the bind mount, run both containers under your host UID and GID. If your UID is not 1000, set BINDERDASH_UID and BINDERDASH_GID in .env first (see Container user ). printf 'BINDERDASH_UID=%s\nBINDERDASH_GID=%s\n' "$(id -u)" "$(id -g)" >> .env docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build # App: http://localhost:8001 docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml logs -f binderdash # backend logs docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml logs -f frontend-watcher # frontend build logs docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml down Troubleshooting commands: docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml ps docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml exec binderdash ls -la /app/backend/ docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml exec frontend-watcher ls -la /app/frontend/ Production deployment is covered in Docker deployment . Tests ¶ Backend unit tests (pytest): cd backend pytest # all tests pytest tests/test_dna_optimization.py -k name -x # a single test End-to-end tests (Playwright), which start the servers defined in playwright.config.js : pnpm test See tests/README.md for details of the end-to-end workflow tests. Documentation ¶ The docs are built with MkDocs and versioned with mike . To preview locally: pip install -r requirements-docs.txt mkdocs serve The docs GitHub Actions workflow publishes to GitHub Pages on every push: Push to Published as main main , aliased to latest (the default version) develop develop a vX.Y.Z tag X.Y.Z README hero image ¶ docs/images/binderdash-hero.png is composed from screenshots of a running instance. The scripts that produce it are in docs/images/hero/ ; see the header comment in capture.js for the steps. Contributing ¶ Python: type hints, standard import order, log to stderr. Vue: Composition API, with .vue sections ordered <template> , <script> , <style> . Add an entry to CHANGELOG.md for notable features and fixes. Releases: see the Releasing section of AGENTS.md . The app version in backend/pyproject.toml must match the vX.Y.Z tag.

docs.text: Storage architecture ¶ Binderdash stores data in three locations: a server-side database, browser IndexedDB, and the server filesystem. Use this reference when planning backups, multi-user deployments, or container rebuilds. For backup procedures, see Backup and restore . 1. Server-side database (SQLite by default) ¶ The DATABASE environment variable (see AGENTS.md , resolved in backend/persistence/factory.py ) selects the database backend. When DATABASE is unset, Binderdash uses NoopDesignsRepository , disables database persistence (which also disables per-user API keys), and serves data from the in-memory cache populated by startup filesystem scans. With DATABASE=sqlite:///path/to/file (or the default backend/data/binderdash.sqlite ), backend/persistence/sqlite_repo.py creates these tables: Table Contents binderdash_runs Run-level metadata: method, run name, project ID, resolved run path, ingested_at , and a run_json blob. binderdash_designs Per-design records with indexed columns ( run_id , design_id , tag , good , binder_chain , short_name ), a data_json blob for method-specific score columns, and extra_data for user-added fields. Startup reads this table into the in-memory designs_cache (see cache.py ). binderdash_users User accounts: email, display name, picture URL, is_admin , is_active , and first/last login timestamps. Non-null emails are unique and link logins across auth providers. binderdash_user_identities Auth identities per (provider, identifier) mapped to binderdash_users . Credentials are stored separately in LOCAL_USERS bcrypt hashes or delegated to PAM or Google OAuth. binderdash_api_keys Per-user API keys: name, key prefix, key_hash , and created/expires/revoked/last-used timestamps. Key names are unique among active keys for a given user. binderdash_auth_users Legacy login-audit table kept for backward compatibility. Startup migrations copy existing rows into binderdash_users and binderdash_user_identities . binderdash_tag_metrics_cache Cached tag-placement metrics (SASA-based tag-site scoring), keyed by run, design, structure file, and tag parameters to avoid recomputing repeated UI requests. binderdash_structural_metrics_cache Cached structural metrics from backend/filtering/structural_metrics.py (secondary structure, hydrophobic patch area, hbonds/saltbridges, delta SASA), keyed by run, design, structure file, and chain selection. binderdash_target_contacts_cache Cached per-design target contact records, keyed by run, design, structure file, chains, and a parameter hash ( params_key ). binderdash_target_residues Per-run target residue reference data and target_moves flag, keyed by run, params_key , and chains. binderdash_saved_sets Named Saved Sets created from the Filtering tab: id, name, creation timestamp, source run IDs, filter/ranking/diversity recipe ( filter_params JSON), and result_summary JSON. Saved Sets are stored server-side, shared across all users of the server/database, and unaffected by clearing browser data. binderdash_saved_set_designs Designs belonging to each Saved Set at creation time: design/run/source-path identifiers, final rank, quality score, diversity-subset membership, and a metrics snapshot. Saved Sets are immutable after creation except for renaming ( PATCH /api/saved-sets/{id} ); clicking "reapply filters" in the UI creates a new set instead of editing the existing one. None of these tables store structure files (PDB/CIF) or raw run output. They store only metadata, computed metrics, and filesystem paths pointing to the server files in §3. SQLite is the only implemented backend. docs.text: Authentication Setup ¶ Binderdash supports five authentication modes: Auth disabled (public API) Session auth via local bcrypt users Session auth via PAM (Unix accounts) Session auth via Google OAuth (OIDC) Per-user API key auth for scripted access You can enable multiple auth providers at the same time. Quick Reference ¶ DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="true" makes all protected endpoints public and bypasses provider checks. Session auth uses cookies ( binderdash_session ) and CSRF protection for non-GET requests. API key auth uses Authorization: Bearer <key> or X-Binderdash-Api-Key: <key> . Keys are per-user, named, expiring, and revocable (there is no shared server secret) and require DATABASE . Username/password login ( POST /api/auth/login ) checks local users first, then PAM (if enabled). Google OAuth signs in through /api/auth/google/login and creates the same session cookies as local/PAM login. Every successful login resolves to a user (see User model and admin allowlist ); BINDERDASH_ADMIN_USERS is re-applied on every startup and login. Environment Variables ¶ Auth-related variables supported in .env.example : DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION LOCAL_USERS PAM_LOCAL_ENABLED PAM_LOCAL_ALLOWED_USERS PAM_LOCAL_SERVICE PAM_GECOS_EMAIL GOOGLE_AUTH_ENABLED GOOGLE_AUTH_CLIENT_ID GOOGLE_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET GOOGLE_AUTH_REDIRECT_URI GOOGLE_AUTH_ALLOWED_USERS SECRET_KEY ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES BINDERDASH_ADMIN_USERS DATABASE (required for per-user API keys) Provider Precedence and Coexistence ¶ When multiple options are enabled: Global override: if DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="true" , auth is bypassed for protected routes. Protected API route auth (when auth is enabled): API key is checked first. If no valid API key is present, session cookie auth is checked. Username/password login flow ( POST /api/auth/login ): Local bcrypt users are checked first. PAM is checked only if local auth did not match and PAM_LOCAL_ENABLED="true" . Google OAuth flow: Independent login path that issues session cookies on success. Protected routes then follow the API key and cookie precedence above. Auth Type 1: Disable Authentication (Public Mode) ¶ Use this for local development only. DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="true" Notes: Protected endpoints no longer require login, API key, or CSRF. You can leave other auth variables set; they are effectively bypassed while this is true . Auth Type 2: Local Username/Password (bcrypt) ¶ Enable local session login with bcrypt hashes in LOCAL_USERS . Step 1: Generate bcrypt hashes ¶ python backend/scripts/encrypt_password.py alice python backend/scripts/encrypt_password.py bob Step 2: Set LOCAL_USERS ¶ LOCAL_USERS="alice:$2b$12$...,bob:$2b$12$..." DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Step 3: Login ¶ POST /api/auth/login Content-Type: application/json { "username": "alice", "password": "your-password" } Successful login returns user details plus csrf_token , and sets session cookies. Auth Type 3: PAM Username/Password (Unix Accounts) ¶ Enable PAM-based login for allowed system users. PAM_LOCAL_ENABLED="true" PAM_LOCAL_ALLOWED_USERS="ubuntu,bob,alice" # comma-separated list, or "*" for any PAM-valid user PAM_LOCAL_SERVICE="common-auth" DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Important: PAM login is attempted only after local user auth fails. PAM_LOCAL_ALLOWED_USERS is required in practice ( * or a comma-separated allowlist; case-insensitive). In containers, host users usually do not exist unless explicitly provided. PAM with Docker Compose (required host account binds) ¶ When Binderdash runs in Docker, PAM checks the container's user database by default. That usually includes only container users (for example app ), not host users like perry . To authenticate host Linux users through PAM in Docker, you must bind host account files read-only: services: binderdash: volumes: - /etc/passwd:/etc/passwd:ro - /etc/group:/etc/group:ro - /etc/shadow:/etc/shadow:ro group_add: - "42" # gid `shadow` - see below; without it every login fails The mounts are active in docker-compose.dev.yml and commented out in docker-compose.yml . Requiring the shadow group ¶ pam_unix delegates /etc/shadow lookups to /sbin/unix_chkpwd . Although that helper is setgid shadow , it only uses that privilege when checking the calling user's own password, preventing unprivileged processes from brute-forcing other accounts. Because the container runs as a non-root user: , every login for another account is a cross-user check, and /sbin/unix_chkpwd returns PAM_AUTHINFO_UNAVAIL . pam_unix reports this as a standard authentication error ( "Incorrect username or password" ), even with a valid password. Adding gid 42 grants the container process direct read access to /etc/shadow . To diagnose the failure inside the container, run the helper directly: docker compose exec binderdash sh -c 'printf %s "$PW" | /sbin/unix_chkpwd someuser nullok; echo $?' # 9 = cannot read /etc/shadow (missing shadow group) # 7 = read it fine, password genuinely wrong Recreating the container after host account changes ¶ Single-file bind mounts attach to the original file's inode. Because passwd(1) replaces /etc/shadow with a new file instead of editing it in place, a running container continues reading the old version. Password updates and new host users will not appear in the container, and logins will check against stale hashes. Running docker compose restart keeps the same container and mounts, so it will not reload the file. Compare md5sum /etc/shadow on the host and inside the container to verify, then recreate the container: docker compose up -d --force-recreate Recommended matching env: PAM_LOCAL_ENABLED="true" PAM_LOCAL_ALLOWED_USERS="bob,alice" # comma-separated list, or "*" for broader access PAM_LOCAL_SERVICE="common-auth" DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" After changing compose mounts or env values, recreate the container so PAM sees the updated runtime: docker compose up -d --build Security note: Mounting /etc/shadow into a container exposes password-hash data to that container. Use this only on trusted development hosts, with minimal container access. For safer container auth in many cases, prefer LOCAL_USERS (bcrypt) instead of PAM. Auth Type 4: Google OAuth (OIDC) ¶ Enable Google sign-in and restrict it to allowed emails. Step 1: Configure Google credentials ¶ GOOGLE_AUTH_ENABLED="true" GOOGLE_AUTH_CLIENT_ID="..." GOOGLE_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET="..." GOOGLE_AUTH_REDIRECT_URI="http://localhost:8000/api/auth/google/callback" GOOGLE_AUTH_ALLOWED_USERS="user1@example.com,user2@example.com" DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Step 2: Configure redirect URI in Google Cloud ¶ Your Google OAuth client must include the same callback URI as GOOGLE_AUTH_REDIRECT_URI . Step 3: Start login flow ¶ Open: /api/auth/google/login Notes: Google auth is considered configured only when enabled and client ID/secret/redirect URI are all non-empty. If GOOGLE_AUTH_ALLOWED_USERS is empty, Google sign-in is effectively denied for everyone. Successful callback issues the same session cookies as local/PAM login. Auth Type 5: Per-User API Key ¶ Use this for scripts/agents without browser session or CSRF handling. Per-user API keys are enabled automatically whenever DATABASE is configured (no separate feature flag is required): DATABASE="sqlite:///./binderdash.db" # or Postgres URL; keys are stored in the DB DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Create a user and an API key in the web UI (top-right account menu, API keys ) or via the CLI: python -m backend.cli user create --email you@example.org --admin python -m backend.cli key create you@example.org --name bootstrap The CLI writes the token to stdout and prints a warning to stderr. The raw token is displayed once because the server stores only its SHA-256 hash. Other CLI subcommands include user list|show|link-identity|set-admin and key list|revoke . Use either header format: Authorization: Bearer <token> or X-Binderdash-Api-Key: <token> Notes: For state-changing requests, API key auth bypasses CSRF checks. On protected routes, a valid API key is accepted before cookie auth. /api/auth/me requires cookie session auth (it does not accept API key auth). Each key has a name, an optional expiry ( --expires-days ), and can be revoked immediately with key revoke <id> . With no DATABASE configured, GET /api/auth/status reports api_keys.enabled: false, reason: "persistence_disabled" and the key-management endpoints return 503 . Key management requires a browser session. GET/POST /api/api-keys and PATCH/DELETE /api/api-keys/{id} return 403 for API-key-authenticated requests so a compromised key cannot create replacements or list other keys. GET /api/users also requires admin privileges. User model and admin allowlist ¶ A user represents one person, and an identity represents one login method keyed by (provider, identifier) (for example, local:alice , pam:alice , or google:alice@example.org ). Binderdash creates a user automatically on the first successful login. Two identities merge into the same user only when they share a verified email address. For example, PAM login for alice and Google login for alice@example.org merge only when PAM_GECOS_EMAIL resolves to the same address (see below); otherwise they remain separate users. BINDERDASH_ADMIN_USERS is a comma-separated allowlist that grants is_admin . Entries match a user's email, provider:identifier pair, or plain username. Unlike PAM_LOCAL_ALLOWED_USERS , this variable does not support a * wildcard, preventing accidental admin grants to all users. Binderdash re-applies this allowlist on every startup and login. To revoke admin access, remove the entry and restart or wait for the user's next login. Admin status granted via python -m backend.cli user set-admin will be overwritten unless the user is also listed in BINDERDASH_ADMIN_USERS . PAM_GECOS_EMAIL ¶ Default: false . When true , PAM login reads the user's email from the 5th GECOS field only ("other") and ignores fields 1-4 ("full name", "room", "work phone", "home phone"). Restricting to the 5th field prevents account takeover. Standard Linux configurations set CHFN_RESTRICT="rwh" in /etc/login.defs , allowing local users to edit their room, work phone, and home phone via chfn . Because chfn has no flag for the 5th field and rejects commas in input, only root can set that field. Reading any user-writable field would allow a shell user to enter another user's email with chfn , merge into that Binderdash account, and gain access to its API keys and admin privileges. Session and CSRF Behaviour ¶ When auth is enabled and you use session cookies: Server sets: binderdash_session (HttpOnly session token) binderdash_csrf (readable cookie) For non-GET/HEAD/OPTIONS requests, send X-CSRF-Token matching binderdash_csrf . CSRF checks are skipped for: /api/auth/login /api/auth/logout /api/auth/status /api/auth/google/login /api/auth/google/callback Any request with a valid API key Verify Active Providers ¶ Use: GET /api/auth/status Response shape: { "auth_disabled": false, "desktop_mode": false, "providers": { "local": { "enabled": true }, "pam": { "enabled": false }, "google": { "enabled": true, "login_url": "/api/auth/google/login" } }, "api_keys": { "enabled": true, "reason": null } } api_keys.reason is null when keys are enabled, "auth_disabled" when DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION=true (keys require user accounts), or "persistence_disabled" when DATABASE is unset. Recommended Combinations ¶ Local dev (public): DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="true" Team dev (session login): local users and/or PAM, DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Production user login: Google OAuth + allowlist, DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Automation access: configure DATABASE , then create per-user keys via the UI or python -m backend.cli key create (works alongside any session provider)

docs.text: Use this for scripts/agents without browser session or CSRF handling. Per-user API keys are enabled automatically whenever DATABASE is configured (no separate feature flag is required): DATABASE="sqlite:///./binderdash.db" # or Postgres URL; keys are stored in the DB DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION="false" Create a user and an API key in the web UI (top-right account menu, API keys ) or via the CLI: python -m backend.cli user create --email you@example.org --admin python -m backend.cli key create you@example.org --name bootstrap The CLI writes the token to stdout and prints a warning to stderr. The raw token is displayed once because the server stores only its SHA-256 hash. Other CLI subcommands include user list|show|link-identity|set-admin and key list|revoke . Use either header format: Authorization: Bearer <token> or X-Binderdash-Api-Key: <token> Notes: For state-changing requests, API key auth bypasses CSRF checks. On protected routes, a valid API key is accepted before cookie auth. /api/auth/me requires cookie session auth (it does not accept API key auth). Each key has a name, an optional expiry ( --expires-days ), and can be revoked immediately with key revoke <id> . With no DATABASE configured, GET /api/auth/status reports api_keys.enabled: false, reason: "persistence_disabled" and the key-management endpoints return 503 . Key management requires a browser session. GET/POST /api/api-keys and PATCH/DELETE /api/api-keys/{id} return 403 for API-key-authenticated requests so a compromised key cannot create replacements or list other keys. GET /api/users also requires admin privileges.
docs.title: Auth Type 5: Per-User API Key

docs.text: A user represents one person, and an identity represents one login method keyed by (provider, identifier) (for example, local:alice , pam:alice , or google:alice@example.org ). Binderdash creates a user automatically on the first successful login. Two identities merge into the same user only when they share a verified email address. For example, PAM login for alice and Google login for alice@example.org merge only when PAM_GECOS_EMAIL resolves to the same address (see below); otherwise they remain separate users. BINDERDASH_ADMIN_USERS is a comma-separated allowlist that grants is_admin . Entries match a user's email, provider:identifier pair, or plain username. Unlike PAM_LOCAL_ALLOWED_USERS , this variable does not support a * wildcard, preventing accidental admin grants to all users. Binderdash re-applies this allowlist on every startup and login. To revoke admin access, remove the entry and restart or wait for the user's next login. Admin status granted via python -m backend.cli user set-admin will be overwritten unless the user is also listed in BINDERDASH_ADMIN_USERS .
docs.title: User model and admin allowlist

docs.text: Default: false . When true , PAM login reads the user's email from the 5th GECOS field only ("other") and ignores fields 1-4 ("full name", "room", "work phone", "home phone"). Restricting to the 5th field prevents account takeover. Standard Linux configurations set CHFN_RESTRICT="rwh" in /etc/login.defs , allowing local users to edit their room, work phone, and home phone via chfn . Because chfn has no flag for the 5th field and rejects commas in input, only root can set that field. Reading any user-writable field would allow a shell user to enter another user's email with chfn , merge into that Binderdash account, and gain access to its API keys and admin privileges.

docs.text: Desktop app ¶ The desktop app is the full Binderdash interface in a native window, for use on a single machine. It needs no server, Docker or sign-in: it stores its database in your user profile and reads run folders directly from your disk. Download and install ¶ Download the file for your platform from the latest release . The builds are not code-signed, so macOS and Windows ask you to confirm the first launch. Linux ¶ Download Binderdash-<version>-x86_64.AppImage , make it executable and run it: chmod +x Binderdash-*-x86_64.AppImage ./Binderdash-*-x86_64.AppImage The AppImage needs the system WebKitGTK and GTK 3 libraries (on Debian/Ubuntu: libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 and libgtk-3-0 ) and FUSE ( libfuse2 ) to mount itself. macOS (Apple silicon) ¶ Unzip Binderdash-<version>-macos-arm64.zip . Double-click Binderdash.app . If macOS blocks the app, right-click it and choose Open , or clear the quarantine flag: xattr -cr Binderdash.app Windows ¶ Unzip Binderdash-<version>-win64.zip anywhere. Run Binderdash.exe . The app uses the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime , which is already installed on current Windows 10 and 11. If SmartScreen warns about an unsigned app, choose More info , then Run anyway . Loading your runs ¶ Open Ingest Runs and use Choose folder to pick the folder that contains your design runs. The path is saved for future sessions. Scan the folder tree and ingest the runs you want. Binderdash detects RFdiffusion, RFdiffusion3, BindCraft and BoltzGen output layouts. Tick runs in Select Runs , then explore them in Designs , Plots and Filtering . Ingesting imports run results into the app's database without changing or deleting any files in your run folders. Removing a run from Binderdash only deletes the database record; the original files remain on disk. Data directory ¶ OS Location Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/binderdash or ~/.local/share/binderdash macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Binderdash Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Binderdash This folder contains binderdash.sqlite (the database), desktop.json (folder and window settings), and binderdash.log . If the app fails to start, check binderdash.log first.

Docker deployment ¶ Run Binderdash as a shared server with Docker Compose. Overview ¶ The application is containerized using a single Docker image that: Builds the frontend (Vue.js + Vite) during the Docker build process Serves both the backend API and frontend static files via FastAPI Mounts data directories as read-only volumes for security Includes health checks and resource limits For PAM authentication inside Docker (bind-mounting /etc/passwd / /etc/group / /etc/shadow , the shadow group requirement, and container-recreate gotchas), see Authentication setup . Prerequisites ¶ Host Directory Setup ¶ Before running the containerized application, ensure the directories specified in RUN_BASE_DIRS exist and are accessible on the host. They should contain your protein binder design run data; the container mounts them as read-only volumes. # Example: make directories readable by the container user (see "Container user" below) sudo chmod -R a+rX /data/runs /data2/runs Environment Configuration ¶ Copy .env.example to .env : cp .env.example .env Set the container user to your own uid and gid (see Container user ): printf 'BINDERDASH_UID=%s
BINDERDASH_GID=%s
' "$(id -u)" "$(id -g)" >> .env Configure environment variables in .env : # Required: set the paths to your data directories RUN_BASE_DIRS="/data/runs,/data2/runs" # Optional: Google OAuth allowlist (use with GOOGLE_AUTH_* vars) GOOGLE_AUTH_ALLOWED_USERS="user1@example.com,user2@example.com" # Optional: for local authentication (dev only) LOCAL_USERS="alice:$2b$12$...,bob:$2b$12$..." Docker Compose automatically loads all environment variables from the .env file. Mounting your run directories ¶ Because Binderdash reads RUN_BASE_DIRS inside the container, mount each directory into the binderdash service and list its container path. For example, to serve runs from /data/runs on the host, add a volume to docker-compose.yml : services: binderdash: volumes: - /data/runs:/data/runs:ro Then set RUN_BASE_DIRS="/data/runs" in .env . A read-only mount ( :ro ) works because Binderdash does not write to run folders. Database directory ¶ Binderdash creates the SQLite database in ./data on the host (mounted at /app/data ) on first start. The data/ directory is tracked in the repository, so it already exists after cloning and is owned by your user. Container user ¶ The binderdash container runs as a non-root user configured by numeric IDs in .env : Variable Meaning Default BINDERDASH_UID User ID the container process runs as 1000 BINDERDASH_GID Group ID the container process runs as 1000 This uid and gid own any files created in ./data (the SQLite database and its -wal / -shm files) and need read access to your run directories. Matching your host user ensures: ./data , which you own after cloning, is writable without a chown run directories you can read, the container can read the database files on the host belong to you, so you can back up, copy or delete them without sudo To set them to the user you are logged in as: printf 'BINDERDASH_UID=%s
BINDERDASH_GID=%s
' "$(id -u)" "$(id -g)" >> .env This writes literal numbers such as BINDERDASH_UID=1001 into .env . Do not use $UID or $GID : Compose only expands variables from its own environment, bash does not export UID , and bash defines no GID variable. Writing $UID in .env expands to an empty string, triggers a "UID" variable is not set warning, and defaults the container to 1000 . Check the result with: docker compose config | grep 'user:' If you change the ids after the database exists, give ./data to the new owner and recreate the container ( docker compose restart keeps the old user): sudo chown -R <uid>:<gid> data docker compose up -d The variables are read by Docker Compose only; the Binderdash backend ignores them. They apply to docker-compose.dev.yml too. HTTPS with Caddy ¶ docker-compose.yml runs a Caddy reverse proxy on ports 80 and 443 in front of Binderdash. Set DOMAIN in .env to the server's public hostname and Caddy obtains a TLS certificate automatically. With DOMAIN unset, Caddy serves https://localhost with a locally issued certificate. Also set CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to your site URL, and set a fixed SECRET_KEY so sign-in sessions persist across restarts. Building and Running ¶ Production Mode ¶ # Build the Docker image docker compose build # Or build with no cache (if you need a fresh build) docker compose build --no-cache # Start the application docker compose up # Run in detached mode docker compose up -d # View logs docker compose logs -f # Stop the application docker compose down Development with live reloading ( docker-compose.dev.yml ) is covered in Development setup . Health Checks ¶ The application includes health checks that verify the FastAPI server is responding on /health , run every 30 seconds with a 10-second timeout. # View health status docker compose ps # Test health endpoint directly curl http://localhost:8000/health Resource Limits ¶ The container is configured with resource limits: Memory: 2GB limit, 512MB reservation CPU: 1.0 CPU limit, 0.5 CPU reservation Adjust these in docker-compose.yml if needed for your environment. Security Considerations ¶ Non-root user: the container runs as BINDERDASH_UID : BINDERDASH_GID (default 1000:1000), not root. Read-only volumes: data directories are mounted read-only. Environment variables: sensitive configuration is passed via environment variables instead of baking secrets into the image. Network: only Caddy (ports 80 and 443) is exposed to the host; the Binderdash container listens on port 8000 on the internal Compose network. Troubleshooting ¶ Common Issues ¶ Permission denied on data directories: the container user (see Container user ) must be able to read the run directories and write ./data . Either set BINDERDASH_UID / BINDERDASH_GID to the owner, or make the directories readable: sudo chmod -R a+rX /data/runs /data2/runs Container will not start: docker compose logs binderdash netstat -tulpn | grep :8000 cat .env Health check failing: curl -v http://localhost:8000/health docker compose logs -f binderdash Frontend not loading: Ensure the frontend was built during the Docker build process Check that static files are being served correctly Verify the build output in the container: docker compose exec binderdash ls -la /app/backend/static/ Debugging ¶ # Access the container shell docker compose exec binderdash /bin/bash # Check application status docker compose exec binderdash ps aux Production Deployment ¶ For production deployment: Put a reverse proxy (nginx, traefik, or Caddy; see Caddyfile and DOMAIN in .env.example ) in front of the container. Terminate SSL/TLS at the reverse proxy. Configure logging and log rotation. Set up monitoring and alerting. Manage sensitive environment variables with a secrets manager. Consider Docker Swarm or Kubernetes for orchestration. Example nginx configuration ¶ server { listen 80; server_name your-domain.com; location / { proxy_pass http://localhost:8000; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; } } Environment Variables Reference ¶ Variable Description Default Required RUN_BASE_DIRS Comma-separated list of base directories to scan /data/runs,/data2/runs Yes BINDERDASH_UID Numeric uid the container runs as (see Container user ) 1000 No BINDERDASH_GID Numeric gid the container runs as 1000 No GOOGLE_AUTH_ALLOWED_USERS Comma-separated allowed Google sign-in emails (with Google OAuth) Empty No LOCAL_USERS Comma-separated list of local users with bcrypt hashes Empty No SECRET_KEY JWT secret key (auto-generated if not provided) Auto-generated No CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS Comma-separated list of allowed CORS origins * No DISABLE_AUTHENTICATION Set to true to disable all authentication false No See .env.example for the full, current list of supported variables.

docs.text: Filtering and ranking ¶ The Filtering tab combines all runs selected in Select Runs into a single table. Expand the Available Metrics panel to inspect every column in the selection, including its canonical name, supporting methods, method-specific raw column names, and min-max range. Use the six numbered sections below it to narrow and order your designs. Hard filters and target contacts filter the Designs table as you edit them. Ranking adds a rank column to all designs without hiding rows. Diversity selection narrows the table further when enabled and applied, and Saved Sets store a fixed snapshot on the server. The in-progress recipe (filters, ranking metrics, budget, alpha, size buckets, diversity on/off) is stored in the browser (IndexedDB). A Saved Set is a separate server-side snapshot. See Storage architecture . For the REST API schemas, see Filtering, ranking, and diversity selection . 1. Hard Filters ¶ A design must pass all enabled filters to remain visible. Edits apply automatically after a short debounce, updating both the Designs table and the filter cascade . The status line displays the passing count. Click Disable all filters to turn off every row without deleting your rules; disabled rows stay in the list but are ignored. Each filter row specifies a column, an operator, and a threshold or value: Column kind Operators Value Numeric < , ≤ , > , ≥ threshold Text contains, does not contain, starts with, ends with, equals, not equals, regex text Either is empty, is not empty none Good good, bad, unrated none Text matching for "contains", "starts with", and "ends with" is case-insensitive; "equals", "not equals", and "regex" are case-sensitive. Null or blank values pass "does not contain" and "not equals" filters. The column picker includes canonical metric names ( iptm , ptm , rmsd , pae_interaction , hbonds , saltbridge , delta_sasa ), raw columns, metadata fields ( design_id , project_id , run_name , method , Sequence ), and user-set columns ( Good and Tag ). Good stores the thumbs rating ( good , bad , or unrated ), and Tag stores the terminus choice ( N , C , or empty); both appear in the picker even before you rate or tag any designs. Canonical names map to each method's corresponding column via METRIC_ALIASES in backend/filtering/metrics.py (for example, iptm maps to design_to_target_iptm for BoltzGen, Average_i_pTM for BindCraft, iptm for RFdiffusion3, and boltz_iptm for RFdiffusion when a Boltz pulldown column exists). METRIC_DIRECTIONS in the same module defines default directions for canonical score metrics. Higher-is-better metrics like iptm default new hard filters to > , while lower-is-better metrics like rmsd and pae_interaction default to < . Adding or changing a ranking metric sets the "Higher is better" checkbox from the same map. Unrecognised raw columns keep the default ( < for filters, higher-is-better for ranking). The columns API includes higher_is_better on each entry so the UI reads these defaults dynamically. If a design's method has no equivalent column for a canonical metric, that design skips the filter. If the method defines the metric but the design's value is null, the design fails the filter. Filtering on a missing raw column name fails all rows. As an exception, missing Good and Tag values are treated as unrated or empty instead of failing. Per-replicate BindCraft columns ( 1_pLDDT , 2_i_pTM , ...) are omitted from the picker because they duplicate the Average_* aggregates. Only passing designs appear in the Designs table, but failing designs remain in the ranking pool ( section 3 ) with a lower rank. Diversity selection and Saved Sets exclude failing designs. 2. Target contacts ¶ Target-contact conditions act as additional hard filters computed directly from each design's 3D structure instead of table columns. Use them to require designs to contact, avoid, bury, or expose specific target residues. They apply on the same debounce as section 1 and count toward both the passing total and the filter-pass count used during ranking. Click Compute target contacts to parse structures in the selected runs and cache per-residue contact data. The coverage line reports how many designs have cached data; designs without cached contact data fail all target-contact conditions. Contact caching only records residues within 12 Å of the binder, so the distance threshold input caps at 12 Å. Binderdash groups runs by target sequence, allowing one target to span runs with different chain IDs. When only one target is present, the residue picker appears directly. With multiple targets, each condition group specifies one target and applies only to runs matching that target (designs from other targets skip the group). If you deselect a group's target run, that group matches zero designs until you remove it or select an active target (which clears the selected residue chips). Each condition combines target residues, a comparison operator, a numeric threshold, a measurement qualifier, and a scope. Comparison Meaning within X of binder closest approach ≤ X further than X from binder closest approach > X SASA when bound ≤ / ≥ solvent-accessible surface of the residue in the complex ΔSASA on binding ≥ / ≤ drop in that surface on binding Distance uses heavy atoms, Cα, or Cβ. docs.text: The Filtering tab combines all runs selected in Select Runs into a single table. Expand the Available Metrics panel to inspect every column in the selection, including its canonical name, supporting methods, method-specific raw column names, and min-max range. Use the six numbered sections below it to narrow and order your designs. Hard filters and target contacts filter the Designs table as you edit them. docs.text: A design must pass all enabled filters to remain visible. Edits apply automatically after a short debounce, updating both the Designs table and the filter cascade .
